workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§271–274
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§271–274: Ögödei's Kitad campaign, Tolui's offering and the western campaigns
part: §§271–274 — Ögödei's Kitad campaign, Tolui's offering and the western campaigns
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§271–274, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Ögödei consults Cha'adai and sends an army against the Kitad, with Jebe in the lead. Falling ill at Shira-Deg, he loses his speech; the shamans find that the spirits of the Kitad lords will take nothing but a kinsman, and Prince Tolui drinks the water of the curse in his brother's stead, asking him to look after his orphans. Ögödei then wipes out the Altan Qan, posts governors in the Kitad towns and returns to Qara-Qorum. Sormaqan subdues the Baqtad, a decree sets the yearly tribute from that land, and the princes under Sübegetei bring the Qanglin, Kibcha'ud and Bajigid to submission, break Ejil, Jajaq and Meged and slay the Orusud, then turn back leaving governors; a closing note recalls the earlier campaign against the Jurchen and Solangqas (Korea), with Jesüder sent as reserve. A note on the text: the Mongol is a Ming Chinese-character transcription, and the glosses in square brackets are the Ming glossators' own; where the English departs from them or is unsure, the note says so.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.t: Basa Ögödei Qaγan Čaγ̇adai aqa-dur ejetüžü ilerün Čiṅgis Qaγan ečige-jüġen belen-dür saγ̇uba.

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Cha'adai, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
to consult, deliberate (stem inferred from the Ming) (verb) [商量着]
to send, go (verb; Ming 敎去 'make go') [敎去]
Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 (name) [太祖︀]
ready, ready-made (adjective; Ming 見成 'already made') [見成 裏]

sentences.l: Again Ögödei Qaγan, Cha’adai to-elder-brother consulting, sending, Chinggis Qaγan his-own-father ready-in sat.
sentences.i: Again Ögödei Qahan took counsel with his elder brother Cha'adai, and, sending (word), said: “I sat down in what my own father Chinggis Qahan had made ready.
sentences.n: Čaγ̇adai aqa-dur ejetüžü ilerün is a converb pair (“consulting … when sending”); no verb of saying follows, so the speech simply begins at Čiṅgis Qaγan, and the English supplies “said”. Shiratori prints no opening quote mark, and I supply one in the English. Who “sat” is left unstated. I take it to be Ögödei, because the reflexive -jüġen (“his own father”) points back to the speaker and the Ming reads belen-dür as 見成裏, “in what was ready-made”. The other reading, that Chinggis himself sat in readiness, is possible. Ilerün is “when sending” (Ming 敎去); an earlier glossary entry also allows “going”.

sentences.t: Ambar erdem(i)-jer saγ̇uba. keġen ügülegdekü-ju bi.

morph.gloss: how, what (Ming 怎生; sense uncertain) [怎生]

words.reading: 額舌兒迭迷-耶舌兒 erdem(i)-jer

morph.gloss: ending of uncertain force, shaped like an instrumental: by, with
question or assertion particle (uncertain; Ming 有 'is')

sentences.l: How by-skill sat? saying, being-said I.
sentences.i: By what skill did I sit there? That is what will be said of me.
sentences.n: Ambar is “how, what” on the Ming’s word (怎生); erdem(i)-jer is “by skill” (技能依着), taking -jer as an instrumental, which is not certain. Ügülegdekü-ju is passive, “is to be said (to me)”; the -ju is unexplained, and the Ming 被說有 gives only “is said”. The sense is Ögödei’s modesty: he fears the question “what skill put him on the throne?”

sentences.t: Čaγ̇adai aqa-ji žöbšijeġesü Qaγan ečige bidan-u Kitad irgen-ü Altan Qān-(n)i dorγud talbiluγ̇a.

morph.gloss: Cha'adai, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to approve, agree (stem probably žöbšiye-) (verb) [道是呵]
we, inclusive (pronoun; stem bidan- before a case) [咱的]
the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹]
Altan, here the Jin emperor's title (title; altan 'gold') [金]
unfinished (uncertain stem; Ming 未完 'not completed') [未完]
past tense (Ming 了; the ending is back-vowel form of -lüġe)

sentences.l: Cha’adai elder-brother-(object) if-approving, Qaγan father our Kitad people-of Altan Qan-(object) unfinished left.
sentences.i: If my elder brother Cha'adai approves: our father the Qahan left the Altan Qan of the Kitad people unfinished.
sentences.n: Aqa-ji žöbšijeġesü puts “elder brother” in the accusative, which is how the Ming 兄行 道是呵 (“if elder brother says yes”) reads; I treat it as “if he approves (of) it”, with Cha'adai as the one approving. Qaγan ečige is “Father Qahan” in the Ming, here “our father the Qahan”. Altan Qān-(n)i is the Jin emperor (Ming 金皇帝). Dorγud (Ming 未完) is “unfinished”; the stem is not known elsewhere, so the sense is the Ming’s.

sentences.t: Edöġe bi Kitad irgen-dür morilasu keġen ejetüžü ileġesü

morph.gloss: the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹]
to consult, deliberate (stem inferred from the Ming) (verb) [商量着]

sentences.l: Now I Kitad people-against let-me-mount saying, consulting, if-sending,
sentences.i: Now let me ride out against the Kitad people,” he said, taking counsel, and when he sent (the message),
sentences.n: Morilasu is mori + -la- + -su, “let me mount” (the Ming 上馬我). The speech closes at keġen; Shiratori marks no quotation here, so the closing mark is the English one. Ileġesü (Ming 去呵) is “if / when he sends”.

sentences.t: Čaγ̇adai aqa žöbšiježü jaγ̇u alžaqu aγ̇uruγ-tur sain küġün tüšižü moriladqun.

morph.gloss: Cha'adai, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
to hinder, be in the way (stem inferred from the Ming) (verb) [碍事]

words.reading: 阿兀舌魯黑-圖舌兒 aγ̇uruγ-tur

morph.gloss: to entrust, appoint (Ming 委付 'entrust'; the glossary lists this sense beside 'stretch out') (verb) [委付着]

sentences.l: Cha’adai elder-brother approving: what hindering? camp-in good men entrusting, mount-you.
sentences.i: Cha'adai, his elder brother, agreed: “What is there to stand in the way? Put good men in charge of the camp, and ride out!
sentences.n: Here the reply is clear: žöbšiježü (“approving”) is a converb, and jaγ̇u alžaqu is “what hinders?” (Ming 甚 碍事). Tüšižü: the Ming 委付着 means “entrusting”; the glossary lists tüši- “entrust” (Ming 委付着) beside “stretch out”, and the sense here is the Ming’s. Moriladqun is the plural imperative “you (all) mount”. The opening quote mark is supplied in the English.

sentences.t: Bi endēče čeriġüd γarγažu ilesü" keġežü iležüġüi.
sentences.l: I from-here soldiers sending-out let-me-send" saying, sent.
sentences.i: I shall send out troops from here,” he said, and sent them.
sentences.n: Ilesü is “let me send” (Ming 敎出我), iležüġüi is “sent” (Ming 敎去了). By the grammar the speaker is Cha'adai, who sends his own army after the plan is agreed; the text does not say so. Shiratori’s closing mark is kept; the opening is not printed, and is supplied in the previous unit.

sentences.t: Jekes ordos-tur Oldaqar qorči-ji tüšižü

words.reading: 斡舌兒朶思-圖舌兒 ordos-tur

morph.gloss: palace, a lady's camp (noun) [宮殿(每) 裏]
Oldaqar, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to entrust, appoint (Ming 委付 'entrust'; the glossary lists this sense beside 'stretch out') (verb) [委付着]

sentences.l: Great-ones palaces-in Oldaqar quiver-bearer-(object) entrusting.
sentences.i: He put Oldaqar the quiver-bearer in charge of the great palaces.
sentences.n: A bare converb (tüšižü, “entrusting”) closes the paragraph with no finite verb, so the actor is not named. Since §272 opens with Ögödei mounting his horse, I take him to be the one leaving the camps in Oldaqar’s hands. Jekes ordos-tur is “in the great (ones’) palaces”, the plural -s on both words (Ming 大(每)宮殿(每)).

sentences.t: taulai žil Ögödei Qaγan Kitad irgen-dür morilažu Žebe-ji maṅlai ilebe.

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [(人)名]
the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹]
Jebe, a man's name (personal name) [人名 行]
forehead; the vanguard, lead scouts (Ming 爲頭 'at the head') (noun) [爲頭]

sentences.l: Hare year Ögödei Qaγan Kitad people-against mounting, Jebe-(object) forehead sent.
sentences.i: In the Hare year Ögödei Qahan rode against the Kitad people and sent Jebe ahead as the vanguard.
sentences.n: The year is taulai, the Hare year (Ming 兎兒, “hare”); the glossary’s earlier entry for the word has the Ming miswritten 免, but this occurrence is written correctly. Maṅlai is “forehead”, and the Ming 爲頭 (“as head, in the lead”) gives “vanguard”; elsewhere the glossary has the same reading (頭哨).

sentences.t: Tedüi Kitad-un čeriġüd-i daružu qunžiγ̇u baitala kiduγ̇ad

morph.gloss: the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹的]
right up to, until (postposition; uncertain) [堆般 直到]

sentences.l: Then Kitad-of soldiers-(object) overcoming, rotten-wood until, having-slain,
sentences.i: Then he overcame the Kitad troops and slew them until they lay like heaps of rotten wood,
sentences.n: Qunžiγ̇u baitala is the doubtful part. The Ming reads 爛木 堆般 直到, “rotten wood, like a heap, until”, so the bodies lie heaped like rotten wood. Qunžiγ̇u is already in the glossary from earlier (Ming 爛木, “rotten wood”, given in brackets there) and is uncertain; the sense is the Ming’s. The text does not name the one who overcame the Kitad and sent the army out in the next unit: Jebe, sent ahead in the previous section, or Ögödei himself, who is named only at Šira-Deg; the English “he” leaves this open.

sentences.t: Čabčijal-i dabažu žüg žüg qotod balaγad an-u eġereġülün čeriġüd jabuγ̇ulžu

morph.gloss: Chabchiyal, the Juyong Pass (place name) [居庸關 行]
town, city (noun; the plural balaγad has lost the final n) [每]
their (third-person genitive placed after its noun; back-vowel companion of in-ü) [他的]
to attack (stem inferred from the Ming) (verb) [敎攻]

sentences.l: Chabchiyal-(object) crossing, direction direction towns cities their making-attack, soldiers making-go,
sentences.i: He crossed the Chabchiyal Pass and sent his troops out in every direction to attack their walled towns and cities,
sentences.n: Čabčijal is the Juyong Pass (Ming 居庸關). Žüg žüg is “each place”; qotod and balaγad both mean “towns” (Ming 城每). An-u is “their” (Ming 他的), placed after the noun, so the construction is “their towns, causing to attack, the troops causing to go”. The chain of converbs runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: Ögödei Qaγan Šira-Deg-tür baγ̇uba.

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [(人)名]

words.reading: 失舌剌-迭克-禿舌兒 Šira-Deg-tür

morph.gloss: Shira-Deg, a place (Ming 龍虎臺 'Dragon-Tiger Terrace') (place name) [龍虎臺名(行)]

sentences.l: Ögödei Qaγan Shira-Deg-at came-down.
sentences.i: and Ögödei Qahan encamped at Shira-Deg.
sentences.n: The Ming glosses the place 龍虎臺 (“Dragon-Tiger Terrace”). Baγ̇uba is literally “came down”; the house rendering for a camp is “encamped”.

sentences.t: Tende Ögödei Qaγan ebedčin kürtežü aman kelen žabqan alžaγdarun

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [(人)名]
to arrive, come to, be struck by (verb; uncertain) [被到着]
to lose (stem inferred from the Ming 失了; uncertain) (verb) [失了]
to hinder, be in distress (stem inferred; Ming 艱難 'hardship') (verb) [艱難︀間]

sentences.l: There Ögödei Qaγan sickness arriving, mouth tongue lost, in-hardship,
sentences.i: There Ögödei Qahan fell ill; his mouth and his tongue failed him, and in his distress
sentences.n: Kürtežü (Ming 被到着, “being reached”, the passive reading the glossary already allows) with ebedčin “sickness” I read as “fell ill” (“was reached by sickness”), which is an inference. Žabqan (失了, “lost”) is not known elsewhere, and its ending is unclear. Alžaγdarun (艱難間) is “in hardship”. The sentence goes on through the next unit to its main clause.

sentences.t: böġes böġes tölgečin-e tölgeleġülüġešü

morph.gloss: diviner (tölge 'divination' + agent -či + -n, as in qoničin; Ming 卜人) [卜人 行]

words.reading: 脫勒格列兀魯額速 tölgeleġülüġešü

morph.gloss: divination (noun; Ming 卜; stem of tölgele- 'to divine') [敎卜呵]

sentences.l: shamans shamans diviners-to making-divine-if,
sentences.i: the shamans had the diviners divine, and (they found) that
sentences.n: Böġes is printed twice, the Ming glossing both 師公(每); I keep the double and take it as emphasis or a slip. Tölgečin-e is “to the diviners” (Ming 卜人行), and tölgeleġülüġešü is the causative, “if / when (they) had (him/them) divine”; the causee stands in the dative, so the diviners are the ones made to divine. Who gives the order is not stated, and the doubled böġes (taken here as the subject) is uncertain.

sentences.t: Kitad irgen-ü γažar usun-u ežed qād irgen orγo-ban daγ̇uliγdarun balaγad qotod(i)-jan ebdegderün türgün-w adalamui.

morph.gloss: the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹]
sovereign, emperor (noun; plural qād, contracted) [帝每]
household (variant of orγa) (noun) [人烟 自的行]
town, city (noun; the plural balaγad has lost the final n) [城]
walled town, enclosure (noun) [每 自的行]
quick, swift (adjective; the -w is Shiratori's) [緊行]
ada=harm, misfortune, a malign influence (noun; stem inferred from the Ming 作崇 'make trouble') [作崇有]

sentences.l: Kitad people-of land water-of lords, sovereigns, people household-their-own when-plundered, towns-their-own when-ruined, quickly make-mischief.
sentences.i: the lords of the land and waters of the Kitad people, the sovereigns, quickly make trouble when their people and households are carried off and their walled towns are ruined.
sentences.n: Qād is “sovereigns” (house rendering), which I take to be the spirits of the dead Kitad emperors (the Ming says only 帝(每), “emperors”). Türgün-w (Ming 緊行, as with türgen-e below) has an unexplained -w as printed. The reflexives -ban and -(i)jan (“their own”) refer to those lords. Adalamui is glossed 作崇, “make mischief, haunt”; the stem ada (taken as a noun, “harm”, with -la-) is inferred from the Ming alone. This is the diviners’ finding, which they repeat to the Qahan in direct speech below.

sentences.t: Irgen orγa altan müṅgün aduγ̇usun ideġen žoliγ̇a ögüje keġen abidlaγ̇asu ülü talbiran düled türgün-w adalamui.

morph.gloss: substitute, ransom (noun; Ming 替身 'stand-in') [替身]
hortative, first person plural: let us … (front-vowel form)
to divine (stem inferred from the Ming 卜; uncertain) (verb) [卜阿]
not (particle negating present or converb forms) [不]
to let go, slacken (stem inferred from the Ming 放 and from talbiramui below; uncertain) (verb) [放]
the more, still more (adverb; uncertain; Ming 愈) [愈]
quick, swift (adjective; the -w is Shiratori's) [緊行]
ada=harm, misfortune, a malign influence (noun; stem inferred from the Ming 作崇 'make trouble') [作崇有]

sentences.l: People household gold silver livestock food substitute let-us-give saying if-divined, not releasing, the-more quickly make-mischief.
sentences.i: When they divine, “Let us give people, households, gold, silver, livestock and food as a substitute,” the spirits do not let go, and make trouble the more quickly.
sentences.n: Abidlaγ̇asu (Ming 卜阿, “if divined”) has a stem abidla- that is inferred from the Ming, and the “spirits” are the English’s supply (the Ming has no subject). Žoliγ̇a is “substitute, stand-in” (替身). Talbiran (放) is “releasing” (taken with talbiramui below as one stem, talbira-), and düled (愈) “all the more”; both are the Ming’s readings. This unit is put in the present like the units round it (adalamui, talbiramui).

sentences.t: Uruγ-un küġün-eče bolqu-ju keġen abidlaγ̇asu qaγan nidün-jen neġežü usun γujužu uγ̇užu jaγ̇un bolbi keġen asaγtažu böġes öčirün:

morph.gloss: to divine (stem inferred from the Ming 卜; uncertain) (verb) [卜阿]
to open (stem inferred from the Ming) (verb) [(開)着]
to say to a superior, report (verb) [奏]

sentences.l: Lineage-of man-from will-it-be? saying if-divined, Qaγan eyes-his-own opening, water asking-for drinking, what has-become? saying being-asked, shamans reporting:
sentences.i: When they divined, “Shall it be from a man of the line?”, the Qahan opened his eyes, asked for water and drank it; and when the shamans were asked, “What has happened?”, they reported:
sentences.n: Uruγ-un küġün-eče bolqu-ju is “will it be from a man of the line?” (Ming 親的人行中麽有); the -ju is an unexplained question particle. Asaγtažu is a passive converb, “being asked”. The text does not say who asked: I take it that the Qahan, revived, put the question to the shamans, though “the Qahan was asked” is also grammatical.

sentences.t: "Kitad irgen-ü γažar usun-u ežed qād γažar usun(i)-jan ebdegderün irgen orγa-ban daγ̇uliγdarun türgün-w adalamui.

morph.gloss: the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹]
sovereign, emperor (noun; plural qād, contracted) [帝(每)]
quick, swift (adjective; the -w is Shiratori's) [緊行]
ada=harm, misfortune, a malign influence (noun; stem inferred from the Ming 作崇 'make trouble') [作崇有]

sentences.l: "Kitad people-of land water-of lords, sovereigns, land water-their-own when-ruined, people household-their-own when-carried-off, quickly make-mischief.
sentences.i: “The lords of the land and waters of the Kitad people, the sovereigns, quickly make trouble when their land and waters are ruined and when their people and households are carried off.
sentences.n: Shiratori’s opening quote mark is printed here. This is the same finding as above, now in direct speech, with the two causes in the opposite order.

sentences.t: Busu jaγ̇un ber žoliγ̇a ögüje keġen abidlaγ̇asu düled türgen-e žiġürmedemüi.

morph.gloss: substitute, ransom (noun; Ming 替身 'stand-in') [替身]
hortative, first person plural: let us … (front-vowel form)
to divine (stem inferred from the Ming 卜; uncertain) (verb) [卜阿]
the more, still more (adverb; uncertain; Ming 愈) [愈]
to grow more severe (stem inferred from the Ming 愈甚; uncertain) (verb) [愈甚有]

sentences.l: Other anything even substitute let-us-give saying if-divined, the-more quickly more-severe-is.
sentences.i: If they divine, ‘Let us give anything else as a substitute,’ it grows only the more severe, and the faster.
sentences.n: Busu jaγ̇un ber is “anything else at all”. Žiġürmedemüi (Ming 愈甚有, “grows more severe”) has a stem inferred from the Ming. The present tense makes this a general rule of the shamans’ finding, not a past event.

sentences.t: Uruγ-un küġün-eče bolqu-ju keġeġesü talbiramui.

morph.gloss: to slacken, ease (stem inferred from the Ming 放慢; uncertain) (verb) [放慢有]

sentences.l: Lineage-of man-from will-it-be? if-saying, slackens.
sentences.i: But when they say, ‘Will it be from a man of the line?’, it slackens.
sentences.n: Talbiramui (放慢有) is “slackens, eases”, so the trouble eases when the substitute is a kinsman. The subject (“it”) is not stated.

sentences.t: Edöġe žarliγ medemü-že" keġen öčiġešü

morph.gloss: to say to a superior, report (verb) [奏呵]

sentences.l: Now decree knows-indeed" saying if-reporting,
sentences.i: Now the decree — he knows it indeed.” So they reported.
sentences.n: Medemü-že (Ming 知有也者) is “(he) knows indeed”; Shiratori’s closing quote mark is here. The sense of the line is uncertain. The most natural reading is that the shamans close their report by leaving the choice to the Qahan: the decree is his, and he knows what the finding requires. I have kept the Ming’s wording.

sentences.t: žarliγ bolurun: "Dergede köġüd-eče ken bi" kēġesü Tolui köġün dergede büleġe.

morph.gloss: near, at hand (postposition; Ming 根前 'in front of, by') [根前]
is, exists (verb, perhaps a short form of bü-; the same spelling as the pronoun bi 'I'; Ming 有) [有]
conditional: if, when (long vowel as printed)
Tolui, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
near, at hand (postposition; Ming 根前 'in front of, by') [根前]

sentences.l: Decree when-making: "Near sons-from who is?" if-saying, Tolui prince near was.
sentences.i: When he issued a decree: “Who of the princes is at hand?” — and when he asked, Prince Tolui was at hand.
sentences.n: Žarliγ bolurun is “when he issued a decree” (house rendering: “issued a decree”). Köġüd-eče is “from among the princes” (Ming 大王(每)處). Shiratori prints an opening quote at Dergede and a closing mark after bi. Büleġe is the past “was, there was”.

sentences.t: Ügülerün: "Sutu Čiṅgis Qaγan ečige bidan-u deġere aqa-nar doro deġü-ner böġetele

morph.gloss: blessed, fortunate (Ming 洪福 'great fortune'; perhaps su 'fortune' + -tu 'having', but the formation is uncertain) (adjective) [洪福︀]
Chinggis, the title borne by Temüjin from 1206 (name) [太祖︀]
we, inclusive (pronoun; stem bidan- before a case) [咱的]
to be (verb; böġe- before an ending) [有間]

sentences.l: Speaking: "Blessed Chinggis Qaγan father our, above elder-brothers below younger-brothers while-being,
sentences.i: As he spoke: “Our father, the blessed Chinggis Qahan, though there were elder brothers above and younger brothers below,
sentences.n: Sutu (Ming 洪福, “great fortune”) is “blessed, fortunate”. Ečige bidan-u is “our father”, with the genitive after its noun, as with min-u. Böġetele is “while (they) were, although”. Tolui’s long speech runs from here to the shamans’ cue; the speech has one printed quote mark opening at Sutu and one closing at žügerüdkün.

sentences.t: Qaγan aqa-ji čima-ji aγta metü soγ̇oṅγužü irge metü biližü jeke oro-ban beje-dür čin-u čučužu olon ulus-i deġere čin-u ačižu ögbe-že.

morph.gloss: accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to choose, pick out (stem uncertain) (verb) [選揀着]
to stroke, feel, size up (Ming 揣摩) (verb) [揣摩着]
place, seat, position (noun) [位子 自的行]
to point at, designate (stem inferred from the Ming 指) (verb) [指着]
to carry as a load, pack (verb) [擔着]

sentences.l: Qaγan elder-brother-(object) you-(object) gelding like choosing, wether like sizing-up, great seat-own your-body-on your pointing, many people-(object) upon your loading, gave.
sentences.i: chose you, my elder brother the Qahan, as one picks a gelding, sized you up as one sizes up a wether, pointed to your person for his great seat, laid the many people upon you, and gave (them).
sentences.n: The two comparisons are the Ming’s: aγta metü soγ̇oṅγužü (“choosing like a gelding”) and irge metü biližü (“feeling over like a wether”). Oro-ban is “his own seat”, that is Chinggis’s throne, and beje-dür čin-u čučužu is “pointing at your body”. Ögbe-že is “gave, indeed”. The English supplies “(them)” as the object of the giving.

sentences.t: Nama-ji bürün Qaγan aqa-jin dergede ažu umartaγsan-i duradγažu untaraγsan-i seriġülžü jabu keġegdelüġe.

morph.gloss: near, at hand (postposition; Ming 根前 'in front of, by') [根前]

words.reading: 兀馬舌兒塔黑撒泥 umartaγsan-i

morph.gloss: to doze, sleep (stem inferred from the Ming 睡着) (verb) [睡着了的 行]

sentences.l: Me-(object) as-for, Qaγan elder-brother’s near staying, forgotten-thing-(object) reminding, slept-thing-(object) rousing go, was-said.
sentences.i: As for me, I was told: ‘Stay by the Qahan, your elder brother; remind him of what he forgets, rouse him from what he sleeps through, and go on (so).’
sentences.n: Nama-ji bürün: nama- is the oblique stem of bi, and bürün (Ming 有呵) is “as for”. Keġegdelüġe is passive, “it was said (to me)”, hence the quotation within the quotation. Jabu is the bare imperative “go”, which the Ming glosses 行; I take it as “go on so”. Umartaγsan-i and untaraγsan-i are past participles in the accusative: “the forgotten (thing)” and “the slept (thing)”.

sentences.t: Edöġe Qaγan aqa-γ̇an čima-ji aldaγ̇asu bi ken-ü umartaγsan-i duradγaqu;

morph.gloss: to incur a penalty, be at fault, err (Ming 罰/失) (verb) [失了呵]

words.reading: 兀馬舌兒塔黑撒泥 umartaγsan-i
都︀舌剌惕中合中忽 duradγaqu

sentences.l: Now Qaγan elder-brother-own you-(object) if-lost, I whose forgotten-thing reminding,
sentences.i: Now if I lose you, my own elder brother the Qahan, whose forgetting shall I recall,
sentences.n: Aldaγ̇asu (Ming 失了呵, “if lost”) has the glossary’s sense “incur a penalty, be at fault”; here the Ming’s “if (I) lose (you)” fits both the accusative čima-ji and the sense of the speech. I follow that. “If you were at fault” is a possible reading of the verb alone. The question is a rhetorical one, and continues in the next unit.

sentences.t: Ken-ü untaraγsan-i seriġülkü

morph.gloss: to doze, sleep (stem inferred from the Ming 睡着) (verb) [睡着了的 行]

sentences.l: Whose slept-thing rousing?
sentences.i: whose sleeping shall I rouse?
sentences.n: The second half of the pair; Ken-ü untaraγsan-i seriġülkü answers ken-ü umartaγsan-i duradγaqu word for word. The participles in -qu / -kü are “shall I …?”, which the question mark in Shiratori’s printing does not show.

sentences.t: ünen ber Qaγan aqa min-u žöb ese boluγ̇asu olon Monγol ulus önečirekün. Kitad irgen kibqaqun

morph.gloss: genitive: my, placed after its noun
to be orphaned (stem inferred from önečin 'orphan'; Ming 孤獨 'forlorn') (verb) [孤獨了]
ending of uncertain force (taken as -qun/-kün 'would be')
the Kitad, here the Jin state (people name) [契丹]
to be satisfied, content (stem inferred from the Ming 意快足; uncertain) (verb) [意快足]
ending of uncertain force (taken as 'would be')

sentences.l: Truly Qaγan elder-brother my right not if-it-becomes, many Mongol people orphaned-would-be, Kitad people satisfied-would-be.
sentences.i: In truth, if things do not go right with my elder brother the Qahan, the many Mongol people would be left as orphans, and the Kitad people would be content.
sentences.n: Doubtful. Qaγan aqa min-u žöb ese boluγ̇asu is, word for word, “Qahan elder brother my right not if-becomes”; the Ming (皇帝兄 我的 是 不 做呵) gives no more. I take it as “if it does not turn out right for my brother the Qahan”, which suits the context of his illness; “if my word is not done right” is another reading. Önečirekün and kibqaqun share an ending (-kün / -qun) that I render “would be”; its force is not clear.

sentences.t: Qaγan aqa-juγ̇an orun-a bi bolsu

morph.gloss: reflexive-possessive: one's own (after a vowel, back-vowel form)
place, stead (noun; Ming 替代) [替代行]
dative: in the place of (back-vowel form)

sentences.l: Qaγan elder-brother-own in-stead I be-let:
sentences.i: Let me be in the stead of my own elder brother the Qahan:
sentences.n: Orun-a (Ming 替代行) is “in the place of”; bolsu is the first-person optative, “let me be”.

sentences.t: Tulu-jin nirγ̇un bi tulbalba. Kileme-jin nirγ̇un bi kiṅgülbe.

morph.gloss: a fish (name; Ming 魚名) [魚名 的]
to split, cleave (stem inferred from the Ming 劈破) (verb) [劈破了]
a fish (name; Ming 魚名) [魚名 的]
to cut across, sever (stem inferred from the Ming 橫斷) (verb) [橫斷了]

sentences.l: Tulu-of spine I split, Kileme-of spine I cut-across.
sentences.i: I split the spine of the tulu fish; I cut across the spine of the kileme fish.
sentences.n: Tulu and Kileme are glossed 魚名, “fish names”, and nothing more is given; their meaning, and why Tolui lists them, is not clear. Tulbalba (劈破) and kiṅgülbe (橫斷) are the Ming’s verbs, “split open” and “cut across”. It reads like a boast of strength, or a riddling description of a victim; I do not guess further.

sentences.t: Ile-ji bi. ilaγba. Γada-ji bi qadquba.

morph.gloss: front, in sight (noun; Ming 面前 'in front') [面前 行]
outside (noun; Ming 在外) [在外 行]
to stab, pierce (stem inferred from the Ming 刺) (verb) [刺了]

sentences.l: In-front-(object) I overcame, outside-(object) I stabbed.
sentences.i: What lay in front I overcame; what lay outside I pierced.
sentences.n: Ile-ji (面前行) and γada-ji (在外行) are in the accusative, “the front” and “the outside”. Ilaγba is “overcame”, qadquba (刺) “pierced”; the stem qadqu- is known only through the Ming.

sentences.t: Niγ̇ur γoγ̇a nirγ̇un urtu bi kü bi-že.

morph.gloss: to be (verb; stem bi- before -že) [有也者︀]

sentences.l: Face fair, spine long I too am.
sentences.i: Fair of face, long of spine — I too am that.
sentences.n: Niγ̇ur γoγ̇a nirγ̇un urtu is a two-part description: “face beautiful, spine long” (Ming 面美脊長). Kü is the emphatic “too, indeed”; bi-že is “I am, indeed”. This seems to describe Tolui himself in the same terms as the fish above, perhaps as a worthy offering, but that is only a guess.

sentences.t: Böġes arbadqun žügerüdkün" keġežü böġes žügerġešü žügergen usu Tolui köġün uγ̇uba.

morph.gloss: to chant a spell, bewitch (stem inferred from the Ming 呪) (verb) [呪您]
to curse (stem inferred from the Ming 詛) (verb) [詛您]
curse, cursed (verb noun or participle of žüger-; Ming 詛) [詛]
water (noun; the final n lost in print) [水]
Tolui, a man's name (personal name) [人名]

sentences.l: Shamans chant-you curse-you" saying, shamans if-cursing, cursed water Tolui prince drank.
sentences.i: Shamans, chant your spell! Cast your curse!” So he said; the shamans cursed, and Prince Tolui drank the water of the curse.
sentences.n: Arbadqun and žügerüdkün (Ming 呪您 and 詛您) are plural imperatives, “you (all) chant”, “you (all) curse”. Shiratori prints the closing quote mark after žügerüdkün; the shamans’ act takes the form of a cursed drink, žügergen usu (詛 水), “the cursed water”. The stems arba- and žüger- are known from the Ming alone. The English closes Tolui’s whole speech here, with a single outer quote.

sentences.t: Qoram saγ̇užu ügülerün:
sentences.l: A-while sitting, speaking:
sentences.i: Sitting a short while, he said:
sentences.n: Qoram is “a little, a short while” (Ming 暫); saγ̇užu is “sitting”.

sentences.t: "Soγtaba bi.
sentences.l: "Was-drunk I.
sentences.i: “I am drunk.
sentences.n: Soγtaba is the past, “was drunk”; the English uses the present, “I am drunk”, because it is said of the moment. Shiratori prints the opening quote mark here, and the closing one at the end of the speech, further down.

sentences.t: Soγtaqu-ji min-u sergütele önečid üčüged deġü-ner(i)-jen belbisün beri-jen Berüde oin-a kürtele asaraqu-ji Qaγan aqa medetügei.

morph.gloss: genitive: my, placed after its noun
to wake, come to oneself (stem inferred from the Ming 省 'regain senses') (verb) [省間]
younger brother (noun) [弟姪 每 自的行]
reflexive-possessive: one's own (front-vowel form; the (i) is Shiratori's bracketed vowel)
bride, daughter-in-law (Ming 媳婦兒) (noun) [媳婦兒自的行]
Berüde, a woman's name (Ming 婦人名) (personal name) [(婦人名)]
to tend, care for (verb) [擡擧的 行]
to know, take charge of (verb) [知者︀]

sentences.l: Me-drunk-(object) my until-waking, orphans small younger-brothers-own-(object) widow bride-own Berüde sense-to until tending-(object), Qaγan elder-brother let-know.
sentences.i: While I, drunk, am coming to my senses, let my elder brother the Qahan take charge of the orphans, the little ones, my younger brothers, my widowed bride Berüde, and look after them until they are grown.
sentences.n: Uncertain in several places. Sergütele (Ming 省間) is “until / while (I) wake”. Medetügei is “let him know”, which here has the glossary’s sense “take charge of” (Ming 知者). Oin-a kürtele (情行 直到, “until reaching feeling / sense”) I render “until they are grown”; that is a guess at the Ming’s 情. Beri is “bride, daughter-in-law” (媳婦兒), and the Ming marks Berüde as a woman’s name; I take her to be Tolui’s own wife. Belbisün is “widow”, said of her in prospect; it is also possible that belbisün and beri-jen Berüde are two persons (a widow, and a daughter-in-law Berüde), or that Berüde is a plural of beri; the Ming marks it a name (婦人名), so I follow that. The Ming reads deġü-ner(i)-jen as 弟姪每, “younger brothers and nephews”, and I give only “younger brothers”.

sentences.t: Ali ber üge-ben ügüleleġe. Bi soγtaba"
sentences.l: Whichever word-own I-spoke. I was-drunk"
sentences.i: Whatever words of mine I have spoken — I was drunk.”
sentences.n: Ali ber üge-ben ügüleleġe is “whatever my own words I have said” (Ming 那箇也言語自的行說了來). Shiratori prints the closing quote mark after soγtaba; I keep it, so the whole speech runs from I am drunk to this point, and the “saying” that follows is the narrator’s.

sentences.t: keġeġed γarču odču žöb ese boluγsan josun teimü.

morph.gloss: not (particle negating a past action) [不曾]

sentences.l: Having-said, going-out going: right not became custom thus.
sentences.i: So saying, he went out and departed. It was a thing that did not turn out right; so it was.
sentences.n: Doubtful. Keġeġed γarču odču is “having said (so), going out, going”. Žöb ese boluγsan josun teimü is, word for word, “the reason (josun) of not having become right, (is) so” (Ming 是不曾做了的理那般). I read it as a closing comment on Tolui’s departure, and the English “so it was” for teimü is loose; the sense of žöb ese boluγsan (“did not turn out right” or “was not done rightly”) is not certain.

sentences.t: Tedüi Altan Qān-(n)i muqudγažu seġüse nere ögčü

morph.gloss: Altan, here the Jin emperor's title (title; altan 'gold') [金]
to wipe out, destroy (stem likely; Ming 絕 'cut off') (verb) [窮絕着]
boy, lad (Ming 小厮; stem uncertain) (noun) [小厮]

sentences.l: Then Altan Qan-(object) wiping-out, boys name giving,
sentences.i: Then, having wiped out the Altan Qan, he gave the boys names,
sentences.n: No subject is named; by the sense it is Ögödei. Muqudγažu (絕着) is “wiping out”. Seġüse nere ögčü is “boys, name, giving” (Ming 小厮 名字 與着). What is meant by giving the boys names is not clear; it may be a way of taking them into service, or of granting rank. I translate the words as they stand.

sentences.t: altan müṅgün altatai hartu aγ̇urasun tabar alašas seġüses-i an-u daγ̇uližu

morph.gloss: patterned, figured (Ming 紋有的 'having patterns'; uncertain) (adjective) [紋有的]
length of cloth, bolt of silk (noun; Ming (段)子; uncertain) [段匹]
a kind of horse (Ming 淮馬 'Huai horses'; uncertain) (noun) [淮馬(每)]
their (third-person genitive placed after its noun; back-vowel companion of in-ü) [他的]

sentences.l: Gold silver gold-having patterned silks goods alasha-horses boys-(object) their plundering,
sentences.i: and carried off their gold, silver, gold-bearing, patterned silks, goods, alasha horses and boys,
sentences.n: Altatai is “gold-having” (Ming 金有的), hartu “patterned” (紋有的), aγ̇urasun “a length of silk” (段匹). Alašas is the Ming’s 淮馬(每), “Huai horses”; I leave the word untranslated. Seġüses-i an-u (“their boys”) repeats seġüse of the first unit and does not make clear whether these are the same boys.

sentences.t: alginči tanmačin talbižu

morph.gloss: tanma-officer, garrison officer (Ming 官名) (noun; tanma + -či-n) [官名]
to set down, leave, post (verb) [放着]

sentences.l: Scouts tanma-officers leaving,
sentences.i: posted scouts and tanma-officers,
sentences.n: Alginči is “scout, advance guard” (頭哨). Tanmačin (官名) is tanma + -či-n, an officer of the tanma, the garrison or watch force. Talbižu is “setting, leaving, posting”.

sentences.t: Nangiṅ, Žuṅdu žüg žüg-tür balaγasun-dur daruγačin talbižu tübšin tügel qarižu Qara-Qorum-a baγ̇uba.

morph.gloss: Nanjing (Han 南京), a city (place name) [汴梁]
Zhongdu (Han 中都), the Jin capital (place name) [北平]

words.reading: 巴剌中合孫-突︀舌兒 balaγasun-dur

morph.gloss: to set down, leave, post (verb) [放着]
whole, complete, safe (noun or adjective; Ming 安) [安]

words.reading: 中合舌剌-中豁舌魯麻 Qara-Qorum-a

morph.gloss: Qara-Qorum, a place (Ming 嶺北 'north of the range') (place name) [嶺北 行]

sentences.l: Nanjing, Zhongdu, each-place each-place-in towns-in governors leaving, peace safety turning-back, Qara-Qorum-at came-down.
sentences.i: placed governors in Nanjing, Zhongdu and every other place, in the towns, and returned in peace and safety, and encamped at Qara-Qorum.
sentences.n: The Ming glosses Nangiṅ as 汴梁 (Bianliang, the Jin southern capital) and Žuṅdu as 北平 (here “Beiping”; elsewhere 大都); I keep Shiratori’s forms Nanjing and Zhongdu. Daruγačin is “governor, garrison commander”. Tübšin tügel (平安) is “in peace and safety”. Qara-Qorum-a is “at Qara-Qorum” (Ming 嶺北行, “north of the ridge”), with the dative-locative -a.

sentences.t: Čormaqan qorči Baγtad irgen-i elseġülžüġü.

morph.gloss: Sormaqan (printed Čormaqan), a man's name (personal name) [人名]
the Baqtad, a people (people name) [種名]

sentences.l: Sormaqan quiver-bearer Baqtad people-(object) made-submit.
sentences.i: Sormaqan the quiver-bearer made the Baqtad people submit.
sentences.n: Čormaqan is Sormaqan (spelling as printed). Elseġülžüġü is else- (“submit”) with the causative -ġül- and a past ending -žüġü (Ming 敎歸附了, “made submit”); the ending is read as a variant of the past.

sentences.t: Tere γažar sain ed sain keġegdemüi keġen medežü Ögödei Qaγan žarliγ bolurun:

morph.gloss: Ögödei, a man's name (personal name) [(人)名]

sentences.l: That land good, goods good is-said saying knowing, Ögödei Qaγan decree when-making:
sentences.i: Learning that it was said, “That land is good, and its goods are good,” Ögödei Qahan issued a decree:
sentences.n: Keġegdemüi is the passive, “is said”; who said it is not stated. Medežü (知着) is “knowing, learning”. Ed (物) is “goods, wealth”, here the things of that land.

sentences.t: "Čormaqan qorči-ji mün tende tanma saγ̇užu

morph.gloss: Sormaqan (printed Čormaqan), a man's name (personal name) [人名]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
tanma, a garrison or watch force (Ming 官名 'office name') (noun) [官名]

sentences.l: "Sormaqan quiver-bearer-(object) just there tanma staying,
sentences.i: “Sormaqan the quiver-bearer is to stay right there as tanma-officer,
sentences.n: Shiratori’s opening quote mark is printed. Qorči-ji is in the accusative, which the English turns into a subject. Tanma (官名, “office name”) is used as the office, “garrison force” or its commander; I leave it as “tanma-officer”. Saγ̇užu is “staying” (坐着).

sentences.t: šira altan, širamal altatan, naqud, načidud, dardas, subud, tanas, küžüġü urtus köl ündür tobičaγ̇ud külin-ereġüd daγ̇uši-kičidud ačiγ̇an-a qačidud lausasud

morph.gloss: ending of uncertain force (the Ming gives only 黃 for the whole word)
possessive plural: those having … (uncertain; Ming 金有的(每))
whole-gold cloth (Ming 渾金; stem inferred) (noun) [渾金(每)]
gold-woven cloth (Ming 織金; stem inferred) (noun) [織金(每)]
brocade (as in the glossary, there Ming 渾金段子 'whole-gold brocade'; here Ming 繡金 'embroidered gold'; stem inferred) (noun) [繡金(每)]
a Western horse (Ming 西馬 'Western horses'; uncertain) (noun) [西馬每]
a kind of camel (Ming 駝名 'camel name') (noun) [駝名(每)]
a kind of camel (Ming 駝名 'camel name') (noun) [駝名(每)]
load, pack animal (Ming 䭾䭾 'load') (noun) [䭾䭾行]
a kind of mule (Ming 騾名 'mule name') (noun) [騾名(每)]

sentences.l: Yellow gold, yellow gold-having-ones, whole-gold-ones, woven-gold-ones, brocades, pearls, large-pearls, necks long-ones, legs high Western-horses, külin-ereġüd camels, daγ̇uši-kičidud camels, loads-for, qačidud mules, lausasud mules,
sentences.i: yellow gold, yellow gold-bearing things, whole-gold things, gold-woven things, gold-embroidered brocades, pearls, large pearls, long-necked, high-legged Western horses, camels of the külin-ereġüd and daγ̇uši-kičidud kinds for the loads, and mules of the qačidud and lausasud kinds,
sentences.n: A list of the goods of the conquered land, and a hard one. Naqud, načidud, dardas are read from the Ming (渾金, 織金, 繡金: whole-gold, woven-gold, embroidered-gold); the stems naqu and načidu are not known elsewhere, and darda is in the glossary already as a brocade (there with the Ming 渾金段子), so the sense of each is the Ming’s and “brocades” is the glossary’s. The plural endings are printed -d, -ud, -dud, -sud, and I parse them loosely. Tobičaγ̇ud is “Western horses” (西馬), külin-ereġüd and daγ̇uši-kičidud are “camel names” (駝名), qačidud “mule name” (騾名), lausasud “mules” (騾), a Chinese loan; I leave the kinds untranslated. Ačiγ̇an-a (䭾䭾行, “to the loads”) I take as “for the loads”.

sentences.t: hon-dur kürgeġülžü Iren adqun" keġebe.

morph.gloss: to bring to, deliver (kür- 'reach' made causative; uncertain) (verb) [送着]

sentences.l: Year-in sending coming be-you" saying-said.
sentences.i: Have them sent in each year, and keep on coming.” So he said.
sentences.n: Hon-dur (Ming 年裏, “in the year”) I take as “each year”, which is the Ming’s sense. Kürgeġülžü iren is “causing to arrive, coming”; adqun is a-, “to be”, with the plural -d- and the imperative -qun (Ming 有者您, “be (you all)”), so “keep on coming”. Shiratori’s closing mark is printed after adqun.

sentences.t: Sübeġetei baγ̇atur-un gežige ajalaγsad Batu, Büri, Güjüg, Münke teriġüten teriġüten olon köġüd

morph.gloss: Sübegetei, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
to go on campaign (verb) [征進的每]
past participle plural: those who …ed (back-vowel form)
Batu, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Büri, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Güjüg, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
Müngke, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
plural possessive: those having …, and so on
plural possessive: those having …, and so on

sentences.l: Sübegetei Hero-of reserve, campaigners: Batu, Büri, Güjüg, Müngke and-so-on and-so-on many princes,
sentences.i: As the reserve of Sübegetei-Ba'atur, the princes who had gone on campaign — Batu, Büri, Güjüg, Müngke and the rest, many princes —
sentences.n: Gežige (後援, “reserve, rear support”) governs “of Sübegetei the hero”, and ajalaγsad is the plural past participle, “those who campaigned”. Teriġüten (等) is “and so on”, the glossary’s reading of teriġü + -ten, a plural possessive; it is printed twice. Büri is here a man’s name (Ming 人名), though the same word elsewhere means “each”.

sentences.t: Qaṅlin, Kibčaγ̇ud-i, Bažigid-i oroγ̇ulžu Ežil, Žajaγ, Meged balaγasu ebdežü Orusud-i kidužu ülüdtele talaba.

morph.gloss: the Qanglin, a people (people name) [種名]
the Bajigid, a people (people name) [種(名)行]
Ejil, a place (Ming 城名 'city name') (place name) [城名]
Jajaq, a place (Ming here 城名 'city name'; elsewhere a river) (place name) [城名]
Meged, a place (Ming 城名 'city name') (place name) [城名]
town, city (noun; the final n lost in print) [城]
the Orusud, a people (Ming 種名) (people name) [種名 行]
to be left over (stem uncertain; Ming 直盡絕 'right to the last') (verb) [直盡絕]

sentences.l: Qanglin, Kibchaq-(object), Bajigid-(object) making-enter, Ejil, Jajaq, Meged towns breaking, Orusud-(object) slaying until-none, took-captive.
sentences.i: They brought the Qanglin, the Kibcha'ud and the Bajigid to submission, broke the towns of Ejil, Jajaq and Meged, slew the Orusud to the last man, and took captives.
sentences.n: Oroγ̇ulžu is “making enter” (Ming 敎投入着, “had them come in”), which I render “brought to submission”. Ejil, Jajaq and Meged are glossed 城名, “city names”; the same Jajaq is a river name elsewhere in the glossary, and Ejil may be the Itil / Adil of §§267–270, but I keep the Ming’s “towns” here. Ülüdtele (直盡絕) is “until nothing was left”. Talaba is “plundered, took captive”, and the English supplies “captives”.

sentences.t: Asud, Sesüd, Bolarman, Kerman-Kiwa teriġüten balaγad-un irgen-i daγ̇uližu elšeġülžü daruγačin, tanmačin-i talbižu qariba.

morph.gloss: the Asud, a people (Ming here 城名 'city name') (place name or people name) [城名]
the Sesüd, a people (Ming here 城名 'city name') (place name or people name) [城名]
Bolarman, a place (Ming 城名 'city name') (place name) [城名]
Kerman-Kiwa, a place (Ming 城名 'city name') (place name) [城名]
plural possessive: those having …, and so on
to set down, leave, post (verb) [放着]

sentences.l: Asud, Sesüd, Bolarman, Kerman-Kiwa and-so-on towns-of people-(object) plundering, making-submit, governors tanma-officers-(object) leaving, returned.
sentences.i: Plundering the people of the towns of Asud, Sesüd, Bolarman, Kerman-Kiwa and the rest, and making them submit, they placed governors and tanma-officers, and returned.
sentences.n: The Ming glosses all four 城名, “city names”, though in §§267–270 Asud and Sesüd were taken as peoples; the form balaγad-un irgen-i (“the people of the towns”) here favours the Ming, so I follow it. Elšeġülžü (printed elše-) is else- “submit” with the causative, “making submit”. Daruγačin and tanmačin-i are “governors” and “tanma-officers”, as in §273.

sentences.t: Urida Žürčed, Solaṅγas-tur ajalaγsan Žalairtai qorči-jin gežige Jesüder qorči-ji ajalaγ̇ulba.

morph.gloss: the Jurchen, a people (Ming 女眞) (people name) [女眞]

words.reading: 莎(郞)中合思-途舌兒 Solaṅγas-tur

morph.gloss: Solangqa, Korea (Ming 高麗) (place or people name) [高麗 行]
Jalairtai, a man's name here (Ming 人名; the glossary's earlier entry has 種(名) 'people name'; ending uncertain) (personal name) [人名]
Jesüder, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to go on campaign (verb) [敎征進了]

sentences.l: Formerly Jurchen, Solangqas-to campaigning Jalairtai quiver-bearer’s reserve, Jesüder quiver-bearer-(object) sent-to-campaign.
sentences.i: Formerly, as reserve for Jalairtai the quiver-bearer, who had campaigned against the Jurchen and the Solangqas, he sent Jesüder the quiver-bearer on campaign.
sentences.n: The Ming glosses Žürčed 女眞 (Jurchen) and Solaṅγas 高麗 (Korea, the Solangqas); the plural -s on Solaṅγas is as printed. Žalairtai is glossed 人名, “man’s name”, here (the glossary’s earlier entry has 種(名), “people name”), and in the sequence Žalairtai qorči-jin gežige (“the reserve of Jalairtai the quiver-bearer”) I read it as a man’s name, as the Ming does here. Ajalaγ̇ulba is causative, “had (him) go on campaign”.

sentences.t: Tanma saγ̇utuγai" keġen žarliγ bolba.

morph.gloss: tanma, a garrison or watch force (Ming 官名 'office name') (noun) [官名]
optative, third person: let them … (back-vowel form)

sentences.l: Tanma let-them-sit" saying decree made.
sentences.i: “Let them stay as tanma-officers,” he decreed.
sentences.n: Saγ̇utuγai is the third-person optative, “let them sit / remain” (the Ming 敎坐者 adds “cause”). Shiratori prints a closing quote mark here but no opening one; the English supplies it. This second, short decree is separate from the one that closes at adqun. Žarliγ bolba is “made a decree”.
